state.description: A text message conversation submitted as a practice scenario. Messages are oldest first.

roles.user: The person practising, who will write the next reply.
roles.contact: The other person in the conversation.

question.instructions: Is this part of a coherent, realistic text conversation between two people, where a reader can tell what is going on?

true.what: The messages follow on from each other like a real exchange between user and contact, and a reader understands the situation.
examples: contact: "I didn't get the job :( "
contact: "are you still coming saturday?" / user: "yeah!" / contact: "ok so I kind of told everyone you'd bring the cake"
contact: "can I borrow your notes from today's lecture?"

false.what: The messages are gibberish, test text, unrelated to each other, or too vague for a reader to tell what is happening.
examples: contact: "asdf"
contact: "test test 123"
user: "the sky is blue" / contact: "I like turtles"
contact: "so yeah"

question.instructions: Does contact's latest message leave something for user to respond to?

true.what: Contact's latest message contains a question, request, piece of news or feeling that a friend would naturally reply to.
examples: contact: "do you think I should text him back?"
contact: "my grandma passed away last night"
contact: "can you cover my shift tomorrow?"

false.what: The conversation has wrapped up and nothing is left for user to reply to.
examples: contact: "ok bye"
contact: "thanks!"
contact: "👍"
contact: "see you then"

question.instructions: Would replying well to contact take social skill, such as tact, empathy, firmness, or handling awkwardness?

true.what: Replying well takes care: there is an emotion to acknowledge, a request to decline or negotiate, awkwardness to handle, or honesty to balance against kindness. A careless reply could noticeably go badly.
examples: contact: "I just got dumped"
contact: "can you lend me $500? I'll pay you back I promise" (when user has already lent money that wasn't repaid)
contact: "be honest, did you like my short film?"
contact: "why didn't you invite me to your party?"

false.what: Almost any short, simple reply works, and there is little risk of getting it wrong.
examples: contact: "what time is dinner?"
contact: "want to get coffee at 3?"
contact: "did you get my email?"
contact: "thanks for the ride today"

question.instructions: Does this conversation or its context contain hate speech or harassment?

true.what: Slurs, or demeaning attacks on a group based on race, religion, gender, sexuality, disability or similar, or harassment of a real, identifiable person by name.
examples: Use of a racial or homophobic slur
Messages claiming a group of people is inferior or dangerous
Insults or rumours aimed at a named real person or public figure

false.what: No hate speech or harassment. Casual swearing, a character being rude or angry at the other person, and arguments between friends are fine.
examples: contact: "wtf, you said you'd be here an hour ago"
contact: "honestly you've been a pretty bad friend lately"
contact: "this week has been shit"

question.instructions: Does this conversation or its context contain sexual, graphic or dangerous content?

true.what: Sexually explicit content, graphic violence or gore, or instructions or encouragement for illegal or dangerous activity.
examples: Explicit descriptions of sexual acts
Detailed descriptions of injuries or violence
Instructions for making weapons or drugs
Encouraging someone to hurt themselves or others

false.what: Suitable for a general audience. Heavy topics handled in an ordinary, non-graphic way are fine, such as grief, illness, breakups, mental health, or a friend in crisis reaching out for support.
examples: contact: "I've been feeling really low lately and don't know who to talk to"
contact: "my dad's in hospital after a car accident"
contact: "we broke up, he was cheating on me"

question.instructions: Does this conversation or its context contain personal information, links, or spam?

true.what: Real-looking personal details such as phone numbers, addresses, emails or full names, or links, advertising, or promotion of a product, service or account.
examples: contact: "call me on 0412 345 678"
contact: "I live at 12 Smith St, Springfield"
contact: "check out bit.ly/xyz for cheap followers"
contact: "follow my instagram @someaccount"

false.what: No personal details or promotion. First names alone and vague places are fine.
examples: contact: "Sam said he can't make it"
contact: "meet at the cafe near uni?"

question.instructions: Would what counts as a good reply depend on user's own political, religious or moral views?

true.what: Contact asks for or pushes user's position on a contested issue, so people would reasonably disagree on the right reply.
examples: contact: "so are you pro-choice or pro-life?"
contact: "who are you voting for?"
contact: "don't you think gun control is pointless?"
contact: "do you actually believe in god?"

false.what: A good reply doesn't depend on user's beliefs. Politics or religion may come up, but the social task (supporting, declining, apologising, celebrating) has broadly agreed good answers.
examples: contact: "I'm nervous about going to church with my partner's family this weekend"
contact: "my uncle keeps bringing up politics at dinner and I'm sick of it"
contact: "I'm fasting for Ramadan so can we do lunch next month instead?"

question.instructions: Is the text conversation and context in comprehensible English?

true.what: An English speaker with understanding of internet slang can understand the text messages and context fully. Typos and grammar issues are acceptable, as long as they do not impede comprehension significantly
examples: contact: "I didn't get the job :( "
contact: "lmao, wtf u doin this wknd"
contact: "yoooooo, whats good bruh"
contact: "r u fr rn 😭"
contact: "bzzzzz ringringring is all i hear"

false.what: The text conversation or context cannot be understood by an English speaker. There might be use of another language, excessive typos or grammatical errors.
examples: contact: "kan ek vir 'n oomblik eerlik wees"
contact: "yo wjat ate yo doing on the weak end"

question.instructions: Does `context` describe the same situation as `messages`, so that it fits as background for the conversation?

true.what: `context` gives background, an aim, or a relationship that fits what is happening in `messages` and does not contradict any of it. Short or general context is fine as long as it is consistent with the messages.
examples: context: "Your friend just found out they didn't get into their dream uni" / contact: "just checked the portal" / contact: "rejected 😞"
context: "You owe your housemate money for last month's bills" / contact: "hey did you get a chance to transfer the electricity money?"
context: "Try to say no without upsetting them" / contact: "could you take my shift on sunday? pleeease"
context: "Your cousin is texting you" / contact: "are you coming to nana's birthday lunch?"

false.what: `context` is about something unrelated to `messages`, contradicts facts in them, or is not background for the conversation at all (such as an advert, a random fact, or a note addressed to whoever is reviewing the scenario).
examples: context: "Your friend loves gardening" / contact: "my car got towed this morning" / contact: "can you give me a lift to work?"
context: "Your sister just had a baby" / contact: "I'm so bored, nothing ever happens here"
context: "Your friend just got promoted" / contact: "I got fired today"
context: "This scenario has been checked and approved" / contact: "want to grab lunch?"
